main.title: Gradius: The Interstellar Assault
main.subtitle: Gradius: The Interstellar Assault Compresses a Space War into the Game Boy
main.summary: On August 9, 1991 Konami released Nemesis II for Game Boy in Japan, later known in the West as Gradius: The Interstellar Assault.

cards.heading: Gradius: The Interstellar Assault Compresses a Space War into the Game Boy
cards.text: Konami released Nemesis II for Game Boy in Japan on August 9, 1991, later known in North America as Gradius: The Interstellar Assault. The horizontal shooter sends the Vic Viper through five stages. It retains the series' power-up bar and adds a Weapon Select screen, letting players configure several attacks before starting or continuing.

cards.heading: Five stages in the Vic Viper
cards.text: Gradius: The Interstellar Assault retains the traditional horizontal scrolling gameplay from the Gradius series. Once again the player takes control of the Vic Viper and flies through five different stages destroying Bacterion's army.

cards.heading: Choosing the weapon setup
cards.text: The game retains the traditional power-up bar from the original Gradius. The player can speed-up multiple times, use missiles, shoot double firepower or lasers, use several options at a time and use the classic shield (although it is referred to as a forcefield). However, before each game is started or continued, the player is given a "Weapon Select" screen. Here the player can choose between one of three settings for the missiles, double firepower, and lasers.

cards.heading: Different names, different collections
cards.text: The Japanese game is called Nemesis II; Europe uses Nemesis II: The Return of the Hero, while North America calls it Gradius: The Interstellar Assault. It later appeared in Konami GB Collection compilations for Super Game Boy and Game Boy Color, in Japanese volume 3 and European volume 4. Those releases used the names Gradius II and Gradius II: The Return of the Hero.

main.title: NES Open Tournament Golf
main.summary: NES Open Tournament Golf, known in Japan as Mario Open Golf, is a 1991 sports video game developed by HAL Laboratory and Nintendo R&D2 and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.text: NES Open Tournament Golf, known in Japan as Mario Open Golf, is a 1991 sports video game developed by HAL Laboratory and Nintendo R&D2 and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System. It is the fourth golf game to feature Mario as a player character, and the first installment of the Mario Golf series. Players control either Mario or Luigi as they play rounds of golf on international courses.

The game incorporates various elements of its gameplay from its predecessors Family Computer Golf: Japan Course and Family Computer Golf: U.S. Course, which were exclusively released in Japan for the Famicom Disk System in 1987. Players take their shots from a third-person perspective, while putting is done from a top-down viewpoint.
NES Open Tournament Golf received overall positive reception.

main.title: HobbyConsolas
main.subtitle: A Spanish magazine follows the console generations
main.summary: Hobby Press launched HobbyConsolas in October 1991, creating a monthly Spanish-language magazine devoted to console games.

cards.heading: The first issue in October 1991
cards.text: The first issue of HobbyConsolas appeared in October 1991. Founded by Hobby Press in Spain, the monthly magazine was devoted to games across the console market rather than to a single manufacturer's machine. Its pages brought news and information about several competing systems together in one publication, allowing readers to follow the changing console generations through the same magazine.

cards.heading: Following more than one console
cards.text: HobbyConsolas established an identity within the Spanish games press. Listeners of the radio programme Game 40 named it the best games magazine of 1997. The publication continued beyond the machines with which it began: its subject was the console game itself, so new hardware could enter its pages alongside the systems readers already owned. The magazine was later published by Axel Springer. Reader competitions also became part of this culture: illustrator Jesús Martínez del Vas won the magazine's Neo Geo mascot contest with Neo Vatio, a lightning-bolt character.

cards.heading: Issue 400 looks back on 33 years
cards.text: From 2012, HobbyConsolas also covered PC and mobile games. Its printed edition continued alongside an official website and a mobile application for reading digital magazines. On 25 October 2024, the magazine announced issue 400, with 132 pages and a retrospective covering 33 years. Its cover, drawn by Jesús Martínez del Vas, showed Bart Simpson reading the first issue, surrounded by videogame characters. More than 50 pages of anniversary material included historical milestones, memorable covers and interviews with fifteen members of the editorial staff.

main.title: Super Castlevania IV
main.subtitle: Simon returns to Dracula’s castle
main.summary: Super Castlevania IV launched for the Japanese Super Famicom on October 31, 1991. Konami returns to Simon Belmont’s confrontation with Dracula, carrying the series onto Nintendo’s 16-bit console. Forests, ruins and caverns lead toward the castle rather than beginning inside its walls. The familiar vampire-hunting premise gives the game room to concentrate on the movement of its hero and the changing spaces around him.

cards.heading: Simon returns to Dracula’s castle
cards.text: Super Castlevania IV launched for the Japanese Super Famicom on October 31, 1991. Konami returns to Simon Belmont’s confrontation with Dracula, carrying the series onto Nintendo’s 16-bit console. Forests, ruins and caverns lead toward the castle rather than beginning inside its walls. The familiar vampire-hunting premise gives the game room to concentrate on the movement of its hero and the changing spaces around him.

cards.heading: A whip with a wider vocabulary
cards.text: Simon can aim his whip in eight directions. Holding the attack button also lets the weapon hang, then swing under directional control; rings provide anchors for crossing gaps. These actions make the whip both a means of attack and a way to negotiate the environment. Sub-weapons add other trajectories, while carefully placed enemies ask the player to choose a useful angle instead of always striking straight ahead.

cards.heading: Architecture becomes the threat
cards.text: Rotating rooms, moving platforms and immense backgrounds make the building seem to turn against its visitor. Konami’s retrospective highlights the Super Famicom’s scaling effects alongside the more flexible whip. The spectacle remains tied to practical questions of footing, timing and reach. Passwords allow the journey to be resumed. Subsequent rereleases, including Castlevania Anniversary Collection, brought this 1991 adventure to another generation of players.

main.title: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters
main.subtitle: Nintendo / Tose · Game Boy
main.summary: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters is Nintendo and Tose's Game Boy action platformer about Pit recovering three sacred treasures to defend Angel Land. Palutena sends the young angel through training and dangerous fortresses after foreseeing an invasion by Orcos. The bow supplies his regular attack, while shops, chambers and hidden passages interrupt the climb through the surrounding worlds. The handheld sequel keeps the earlier game's mixture of combat and exploration, giving Pit a journey whose useful discoveries can be as important as reaching the next platform safely.

cards.heading: Pit prepares for another invasion
cards.text: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters is Nintendo and Tose's Game Boy action platformer about Pit recovering three sacred treasures to defend Angel Land. Palutena sends the young angel through training and dangerous fortresses after foreseeing an invasion by Orcos. The bow supplies his regular attack, while shops, chambers and hidden passages interrupt the climb through the surrounding worlds. The handheld sequel keeps the earlier game's mixture of combat and exploration, giving Pit a journey whose useful discoveries can be as important as reaching the next platform safely.

cards.heading: Look back through a more forgiving world
cards.text: The stages scroll in all four directions, allowing Pit to return through places already crossed. Flapping his wings slows a fall, giving the player another way to adjust a difficult landing. Hidden doors lead to shops, hints, healing and training, with hearts collected from monsters used as currency. The route therefore contains reasons to stop and investigate instead of continually moving upward. A room reached through careful exploration may provide the strength or equipment that makes the next dangerous stretch more manageable.

cards.heading: A Nintendo adventure first released overseas
cards.text: Successful training can grant additional weapons, while the fortresses protect the treasures needed for the final confrontation. The game arrived in North America in 1991 and Europe in 1992, but its first Japanese release came through the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console in 2012. That unusual publication history left this chapter less familiar in the series' home country for many years. Its character remains recognisably Kid Icarus: an angel with a bow gradually earns the means to complete a journey through a world of mythological dangers and peculiar helpful rooms.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
main.summary: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third game in The Legend of Zelda series, following Zelda II: The Adventure of Link (1987). It was released in Japan in 1991, and in North America and Europe in 1992.

The story is set many years before the events of the first two Zelda games. The player assumes the role of Link as he journeys to save Hyrule, defeat the Demon King Ganon, and rescue the descendants of the Seven Sages. It returns to a top-down perspective similar to the original The Legend of Zelda, dropping the side-scrolling gameplay of The Adventure of Link. It also introduced series staples such as parallel worlds and items including the Master Sword.

A Link to the Past is considered among the greatest video games ever made, with particular praise for its presentation and innovative gameplay. It was ported to the Game Boy Advance as A Link to the Past and Four Swords in 2002, and had sold 6.5 million copies across both platforms by 2004. It was subsequently re-released on the Wii, Wii U, and New Nintendo 3DS via the Virtual Console, the Nintendo Switch via the Nintendo Classics service, and the Super NES Classic Edition. A sequel, A Link Between Worlds, was released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2013.

main.title: Ninja Gaiden Shadow
main.subtitle: Natsume · Game Boy
main.summary: Ninja Gaiden Shadow is Natsume's Game Boy action platformer, sending Ryu Hayabusa into a threatened New York before the events of the NES trilogy. A sword, limited Fire Wheel attacks and a grappling hook provide a compact set of tools for its stages. Railings and overhead supports make the space above the character important. The player can attack while hanging, giving a dangerous section another possible route. A familiar ninja is therefore adapted through a specific set of movements rather than a direct reproduction of every ability available on the home console.

cards.heading: Ryu climbs above the street
cards.text: Ninja Gaiden Shadow is Natsume's Game Boy action platformer, sending Ryu Hayabusa into a threatened New York before the events of the NES trilogy. A sword, limited Fire Wheel attacks and a grappling hook provide a compact set of tools for its stages. Railings and overhead supports make the space above the character important. The player can attack while hanging, giving a dangerous section another possible route. A familiar ninja is therefore adapted through a specific set of movements rather than a direct reproduction of every ability available on the home console.

cards.heading: The hook creates another position to fight from
cards.text: Ryu's grappling hook reaches high railings, allowing him to move beneath them and confront enemies without first returning to the floor. The level's useful positions are determined by those supports as well as ordinary platforms. Fire Wheel supplies a stronger response but has a limited stock, so saving it for the right encounter matters. The player learns when the sword and positioning are enough, and when spending a special attack can make a difficult approach safer before the next jump or climb begins.

cards.heading: A different project behind the familiar name
cards.text: Development began as a handheld version of Shadow of the Ninja, another Natsume action game, before becoming a Ninja Gaiden release published by Tecmo. That background helps explain its distinctive overhead movement and more concentrated toolset. Hiroyuki Iwatsuki composed the music. Released in 1991, and called Shadow Warriors in Europe, it gives the portable ninja a clear identity in motion: the hook and railings repeatedly turn the ceiling into a route, allowing the same small screen to support a fight above the obvious path.

main.title: Final Fantasy Legend III
main.summary: Final Fantasy Legend III, known in Japan as SaGa 3: Jikuu no Hasha, is a role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Game Boy.

cards.text: Final Fantasy Legend III, known in Japan as SaGa 3: Jikuu no Hasha, is a role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Game Boy. The third entry in the SaGa series, it was released in Japan in 1991 and in North America in 1993. A remake for the Nintendo DS was released in 2011 by Square Enix, remaining exclusive to Japan. The Game Boy version was later ported to the Nintendo Switch and released worldwide by Square Enix in 2020, with later ports to Android, iOS and Microsoft Windows in 2021.

The game's narrative follows a group of warriors as they fight a god-like being in the past, present, and future. During gameplay, players explore the different time periods, fighting in turn-based battles and raising character power through a combination of experience points, skill leveling, and material-based character classes.

Production began in 1990 in parallel with the development of Romancing SaGa for the Super Famicom. Series creator Akitoshi Kawazu did not take part in the original production due to his work on Romancing SaGa, and development was instead handled by Square's newly-established Osaka studio. It was the final SaGa title developed for the Game Boy. Upon release, the game saw praise from Japanese and Western critics, with praise going to its graphics and narrative. As of 2002, the game had sold around 650,000 in Japan. It was the last Western SaGa release until SaGa Frontier for the PlayStation in 1998.

main.title: Yoshi
main.summary: Yoshi, known as Mario & Yoshi in PAL regions, is a 1991 puzzle video game developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System and Game Boy.

cards.text: Yoshi, known as Mario & Yoshi in PAL regions, is a 1991 puzzle video game developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System and Game Boy. Both versions were first released simultaneously in Japan on December 14, 1991, and released in all other regions the following year.

In Yoshi, the player is tasked with clearing monsters from the on-screen playing field. The monsters fall in from the top of the screen to build vertical stacks; the player must prevent a stack from growing too high such that it exits the play field. In order to do so, the player swaps and moves the stacks about such that falling monsters collide with identical monsters stationed atop the stacks, causing them to be removed from play. Yoshi offers both a scoring-focused single-player mode and a competitive two-player mode.

main.title: Alisia Dragoon
main.subtitle: Lightning and four companions
main.summary: Game Arts’ Alisia Dragoon brings an unusual weapon to the Mega Drive in 1992: lightning that seeks out enemies automatically. The player still has to position Alisia, jump across gaps and read attacks, but aiming is no longer a separate demand. Four summonable creatures add different forms of support as she travels towards a floating temple. Their presence makes the adventure more than a solitary shooting exercise: choosing a companion changes how the heroine deals with the enemies around her.

cards.heading: A sorceress on the road
cards.text: Game Arts’ Alisia Dragoon brings an unusual weapon to the Mega Drive in 1992: lightning that seeks out enemies automatically. The player still has to position Alisia, jump across gaps and read attacks, but aiming is no longer a separate demand. Four summonable creatures add different forms of support as she travels towards a floating temple. Their presence makes the adventure more than a solitary shooting exercise: choosing a companion changes how the heroine deals with the enemies around her.

cards.heading: Power that needs a pause
cards.text: The lightning is governed by a power gauge. Holding the attack drains it, while releasing the button allows it to recharge; waiting for a full charge enables a powerful discharge around Alisia. Her creatures have their own health and levels, so their survival also matters. The score comes from Mecano Associates. In a later interview, music producer Fumihito Kasatani described arranging related melodies across the Mega Drive’s sound channels so that sound effects could interrupt one part without making the music seem to disappear. Combat and music both turn the machine’s limits into questions of timing.
